title: Hemorrhagic transformation in patients with large-artery atherosclerotic stroke is associated with the gut microbiota and lipopolysaccharide

Abstract Hemorrhagic transformation is a major complication of large-artery atherosclerotic stroke (a major ischemic stroke subtype) that worsens outcomes and increases mortality. Disruption of the gut microbiota is an important feature of stroke, and some specific bacteria and bacterial metabolites may contribute to hemorrhagic transformation pathogenesis. We aimed to investigate the relationship between the gut microbiota and hemorrhagic transformation in large-artery atherosclerotic stroke. An observational retrospective study was conducted. From May 2020 to September 2021, blood and fecal samples were obtained upon admission from 32 patients with first-ever acute ischemic stroke and not undergoing intravenous thrombolysis or endovascular thrombectomy, as well as 16 healthy controls. Patients with stroke who developed hemorrhagic transformation ( n = 15) were compared to those who did not develop hemorrhagic transformation ( n = 17) and with healthy controls. The gut microbiota was assessed through 16S ribosomal ribonucleic acid sequencing. We also examined key components of the lipopolysaccharide pathway: lipopolysaccharide, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and soluble CD14. We observed that bacterial diversity was decreased in both the hemorrhagic transformation and non-hemorrhagic transformation group compared with the healthy controls. The patients with ischemic stroke who developed hemorrhagic transformation exhibited altered gut microbiota composition, in particular an increase in the relative abundance and diversity of members belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family. Plasma lipopolysaccharide and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein levels were higher in the hemorrhagic transformation group compared with the non-hemorrhagic transformation group. lipopolysaccharide, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and soluble CD14 concentrations were associated with increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. Next, the role of the gut microbiota in hemorrhagic transformation was evaluated using an experimental stroke rat model. In this model, transplantation of the gut microbiota from hemorrhagic transformation rats into the recipient rats triggered higher plasma levels of lipopolysaccharide, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and soluble CD14. Taken together, our findings demonstrate a noticeable change in the gut microbiota and lipopolysaccharide-related inflammatory response in stroke patients with hemorrhagic transformation. This suggests that maintaining a balanced gut microbiota may be an important factor in preventing hemorrhagic transformation after stroke. HT can occur in response to treatment with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which remains the gold standard treatment for stroke within 4.5 hours, thereby limiting the application of tPA treatment (Powers et al., 2019). However, the identification of patients who are at high risk of developing HT after ischemic stroke is challenging, and currently no reliable therapies are available for reducing the risk of HT, especially post-thrombolysis, in stroke patients (Boltze et al., 2021). Considering the complex mechanisms underlying HT progression, identifying patients who are at high risk of HT and developing effective new treatments for HT are important challenges. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which is produced by many classes of commensal enteric bacteria, can interact with toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on the cell surface, regulate nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB)-mediated transcriptional activation of inflammatory genes, including those encoding tumor necrotic factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and ultimately lead to dysregulation of the inflammatory response (Brown, 2019). These inflammatory genes mentioned above play important roles in the pathogenesis of stroke and are also implicated in the pathophysiology of ischemic lesions (Rayasam et al., 2021). According to a recent study, metabolic endotoxemia promotes LPS-induced neuroinflammation and affects outcomes after stroke. LPS and Escherichia coli ( E. coli ; which belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family) localize to the peri-infarct area and are associated with activation of TLR4 signaling (Kurita et al., 2020). In a clinical study of stroke patients, the levels of LPS-producing bacteria in the gut microbiota were significantly altered compared with health individuals, and pathways involved in LPS biosynthesis exhibited corresponding changes (Guo et al., 2021). LPS-binding protein (LBP) facilitates the extraction of LPS monomers by receptor CD14 (this exists in a circulating soluble form known as sCD14), which in turn contributes to the interaction between LPS and TLR4 (Gorabi et al., 2022). sCD14 can bind to E. coli (Jack et al., 1995) and is activated in microglia/macrophages following traumatic brain injury in humans (Beschorner et al., 2002). The bacterial load in the blood and lungs was reduced in CD14-deficient mice challenged with E. coli (Haziot et al., 1996; Cauwels et al., 1999). Recently, LBP and sCD14 have been suggested as clinical markers of endotoxemia that reflect plasma exposure to LPS in stroke (Klimiec et al., 2016), its comorbidities (Aune et al., 2021), and other neurological diseases (Safadi et al., 2021). However, the association between proxy biomarkers of gut dysbiosis and systemic low-grade inflammation (LPS, LPB, and sCD14) and HT pathophysiology remains unclear. The link between the gut and brain, the “gut-brain axis”, has recently gained increasing attention. The gut microbiota affects ischemic stroke progression by promoting inflammation (Huang et al., 2023). Normally, the host maintains homeostasis with its gut microbiota through immune supervision, nutritional supply, and a barrier system (Rodrigues E-Lacerda et al., 2023). Disturbance of this homeostasis increases stroke risk (Zeng et al., 2019) and leads to worse outcomes (Zhu et al., 2021). Stroke can rapidly disturb gut homeostasis, as indicated by the significant gut dysbiosis observed in relevant animal models (Lee et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) and in stroke cohort studies (Haak et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2023). Moreover, the stroke-induced overgrowth of Enterobacteriaceae, in turn, accelerates systemic inflammation through LPS-TLR4 pathway and exacerbates brain infarction (Xu et al., 2021). Furthermore, intestinal inflammation is associated with impairment of the gut-brain vascular barrier and recruitment of inflammatory cells to distal organs, which is promoted by bacteria-derived LPS (Carloni et al., 2021). In this context, we recently showed that the peripheral immune response in HT after ischemic stroke can be characterized by dysbiosis of the gut microbiota (Huang et al., 2021), implying a reciprocal relationship between dysbiosis and HT. Nevertheless, whether there is a bidirectional interaction between HT and the gut microbiota, especially in stroke patients who develop HT, remains largely unknown. In this study, we sought to determine whether there are differences in the gut microbiota between HT and non-HT stroke patients. Such alterations in the gut microbiota and associated pathways may be early markers of HT risk or may represent therapeutic targets that could be used to reduce the risk of developing HT. Methods Study population Patients who were admitted to the Department of Neurology of Xiangya Hospital of Central South University (Hunan, China) between May 2020 and September 2021 within 7 days of stroke symptom onset were included in this observational retrospective study. We initially identified and screened stroke patients with large-artery atherosclerosis as classified by the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria (Adams et al., 1993); patients with other determined or undetermined stroke etiologies were excluded ( Figure 1 ). The inclusion criteria for this study were as follows: age 18 years; first-ever acute ischemic stroke; not undergoing intravenous thrombolysis or endovascular thrombectomy; and availability of MRI or CT for evaluating HT. Patients with advanced cancer, other internal of neurological diseases, diabetes (type 1 and 2), or gastrointestinal disease (including inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, intestinal surgery, chronic pancreatitis, or other malabsorption disorder) in the past 3 months were excluded. Individuals were also excluded if they had received antibiotics or probiotics within the past 3 months. Attending neurologists assessed the neurological status of each patient daily. Patients underwent baseline neuroimaging and follow-up imaging with MRI or CT within 7 days post-stroke. Finally, 16 target patients with HT and 17 matching patients without HT were included. A control group of 15 healthy subjects without inflammatory diseases or neurological disorders was also recruited via posters and recruitment letters. The same exclusion criteria applied to the stroke cases were applied to the controls. Blood and fecal samples were collected at admission after the initial diagnosis. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xiangya Hospital of Central South University (approval No. 202105220) and all participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki . This study is reported according to the STrengthening the Reporting of OBservational studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement (von Elm et al., 2007). Clinical data collection and detection of HT The baseline characteristics, vascular risk factors, acute stroke management, and other laboratory findings of the included patients were obtained by reviewing their electronic medical records ( Table 1 ). Clinical stroke severity was assessed at admission using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) (Brott et al., 1989). All patients enrolled in the study underwent a brain MRI or CT at hospital admission and showed no evidence of hemorrhage. One or more follow-up brain imaging studies were performed in all patients according to an institutional stroke imaging protocol (Furie and Jayaraman, 2018). Follow-up brain images were taken when there was clinical worsening or 5–7 days after admission to detect HT. CT-detected HT was defined as increased density in an area of low attenuation (Motto et al., 1999). In MRI images, a combination of diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), fluid-attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR), T1-weighting, and T2-weighted imaging was used to detect HT (Renou et al., 2010). The presence of HT on brain image was independently determined by two neurologists who were blinded to the participants' clinical outcomes. When there was a disagreement between the two examiners, a consensus decision was reached after joint review. Laboratory tests Twelve-hour fasting blood samples from the study subjects were collected in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes at Xiangya Hospital of Central South University (Hunan, China) upon admission. Plasma suspensions were centrifuged at 3000 × g for 10 minutes and immediately stored at –80°C until analysis. The plasma LPS concentration was measured with a Limulus amebocyte lysate assay kit (Houshiji Cod Inc., Xiamen, China). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was used for measuring human LBP (Cusabio Science Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China), human sCD14 (Cusabio Science Co., Ltd.), human zonulin (Cusabio Science Co., Ltd.), human matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) (Cusabio Science Co., Ltd.), mouse LBP (Elabscience, Wuhan, China), and mouse sCD14 (Elabscience) concentrations. All samples were assessed in duplicate. Fecal DNA extraction and sequencing Fresh stool samples from subjects were collected within 48 hours of admission and stored at −80°C until analysis. Total genomic DNA was extracted from the samples using the cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) method (Caporaso et al., 2010). DNA concentration and purity were evaluated using 1% agarose gels (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY, USA). The DNA samples were then diluted to a concentration of 1 ng/μL using sterile water. Variable regions V3–V4 of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene were amplified with the following degenerate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) primers: 341F (5′-CCT AYG GGR BGC ASC AG-3′) and 806R (5′-GCA CTA CNN GGG TAT CTA AT-3′). All PCR reactions were carried out with 15 μL of Phusion® High-Fidelity PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA), 2 μM each of forward and reverse primers, and about 10 ng of template DNA. Thermal cycling consisted of initial denaturation at 98°C for 1 minute, followed by 30 cycles of denaturation at 98°C for 10 seconds, annealing at 50°C for 30 seconds, and elongation at 72°C for 30 seconds, followed by final extension step at 72°C for 5 minutes. Equal volumes of 1× loading buffer (contained Synergy Brands (SYB) green) and PCR products were combined and run on a 2% agarose gel to assess the quantity and quality of the PCR products. The PCR products were then diluted to the same concentration and purified with a Qiagen Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Sequencing libraries were generated using a TruSeq® DNA PCR-Free Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) following manufacturer's recommendations, and index codes were added. The library quality was assessed on the Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Finally, the library was sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina), and 250-bp paired-end reads were generated. Sequencing data analysis Sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) using the Upare software program (Uparse v7.0.1001, http://drive5.com/uparse/ ) (Edgar, 2013). Sequences with ≥ 97% similarity were assigned to the same OTUs. A representative sequence for each OTU was identified for further annotation. The Silva Database ( http://www.arb-silva.de/ ) based on the Mothur algorithm was used to annotate the representative OTUs with taxonomic information (Quast et al., 2013). The relative abundance of each component of the gut microbiota was determined. To study the phylogenetic relationships among different OTUs and identify differences in the dominant species among different groups, multiple sequence alignment were conducted using MUSCLE software (Version 3.8.31, http://www.drive5.com/muscle/ ) (Edgar, 2004). Alpha diversity was assessed by two different parameters: the Shannon index ( http://www.mothur.org/wiki/Shannon ) and the Simpson index ( http://www.mothur.org/wiki/Simpson ). These index values for our samples were calculated with QIIME (Version 1.7.0, http://qiime.org/1.7.0/ ) and displayed with R software (Version 2.15.3, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; http://www.R-project.org ). Beta diversity analysis was used to evaluate differences in species complexity among samples. Beta diversity, as determined by both weighted and unweighted UniFrac values, was evaluated using QIIME software (Version 1.7.0). Principal coordinate analysis was performed using the WGCNA, stat, and ggplot2 packages in R software (Version 2.15.3, Vienna, Austria). Principal component analysis was applied to reduce the dimensions of the original variables using the FactoMineR package and the ggplot2 package in R software. A ternary plot of OTU distribution was generated using the VCD package in R software. MetaStat analysis using R software was subsequently performed to determine differences in the relative abundance of components of the fecal microbiomes. Linear discriminant analysis effect size tools (LEfSe) ( http://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/lefse/ ) were used to identify differences in microbial community composition among the groups (Segata et al., 2011). A similarity of percentage analysis was performed using the R package “vegan”. To explore co-occurrence patterns between taxa, network analysis was carried out using the R package “psych.” Finally, functional predictions were made using Phylogenetic Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States (PICRUSt) ( http://picrust.github.io/picrust ) to identify enrichment of Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways (Langille et al., 2013). Animal care and experimental procedures Stroke is a sexually dimorphic disease. According to previous epidemiological data, stroke exhibits sex differences in risk, prevalence, and outcome (Benjamin et al., 2017). The onset of stroke is earlier in men, but the lifetime risk is higher in women (Ahnstedt et al., 2016) The loss of estrogen and other ovarian hormones at menopause may contribute to increased stroke risk. Sex differences in the immune response and the gut microbiota impact stroke recovery (Ahnstedt et al., 2020). To avoid the interference of estrogen, we used male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats in the current study. Fifty-four male SD rats (300–320 g, 7–8 weeks old) were purchased from Hunan SJA Laboratory Animal Co. Ltd (Changsha, China, license number: SCXK (Xiang) 2019-0004) and kept under a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle in standard specific-pathogen–free (SPF) conditions (daily cycles of 12 hours of light at 23°C and 12 hours of dark at 21°C, 50–55% humidity, light intensity of 100–200 lx, and ad libitum access to sterilized tap water and commercial rodent food). After acclimatization for 1 week (two rats per cage), rats aged 7 weeks were randomly divided into sham group and experimental groups of six to eight rats, as follows: HT – infarct with hemorrhagic transformation; non-HT – infarct without hemorrhagic transformation; F-HT – antibiotics-treated with fecal microbiota transplant from HT rats; F-non-HT – antibiotics-treated with fecal microbiota transplant from non-HT rats. The rats were subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), as reported previously (Longa et al., 1989). All animal experimentation protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Central South University (approval No. 2019-0004). All experiments were carried out according to the National Institutes of Health guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the National Institutes of Health (8 th ed., National Research Council, 2011). Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was performed as described elsewhere (Sorini et al., 2019). After depletion of endogenous microbiota by antibiotics (vancomycin 0.5 g/L, ampicillin 1 g/L, metronidazole 1 g/L, neomycin sulfate 1 g/L; all from Meilun Biotechnology, Dalian, China) for 2 weeks, the rats were given freshly extracted fecal microbiota from HT or non-HT rats by oral gavage once a day. To obtain inoculants, 1 g of fresh feces from donor rats was pooled and suspended in 5 mL sterile PBS. The mixture was vortexed and centrifuged for 3 minutes at 1000 × g , and the isolated supernatant was immediately given to recipient rats by oral gavage. Fresh feces were prepared within 15 minutes before oral gavage on the day of fecal transplantation. After administration of fecal extract for 2 consecutive weeks, the recipients were subjected to MCAO. The rats were humanely euthanized with an overdose of 3% sodium pentobarbital (300 mg/kg, i.p., Nembutal, Ovation Pharmaceuticals Inc. Deerfield, IL, USA) on the 5 th day after the MCAO procedure, and blood, cecal content, and colon samples were collected for next analysis. The LPS and LBP levels in the plasma were detected with ELISA, as described above. MCAO procedure and HT model HT was induced as previously described (Hafez et al., 2015). Rats received 50% dextrose (6 mL/kg) intraperitoneally 15 minutes before middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) to induce acute hyperglycemia. Blood glucose was measured via the tail vein using a glucometer (Freestyle, Alameda, CA, USA). During surgery and the postoperative period, rectal temperature was maintained at 37.0°C using a feedback-controlled heating pad. Focal cerebral ischemia was induced as previously described (Guo et al., 2016). In brief, 90-minute MCAO was performed under anesthesia via inhalation of 2% isoflurane (RWD Life Science, Shenzhen, China) followed by up to 5 days of reperfusion. To expose the common carotid artery, external carotid artery (ECA), and internal carotid artery, a midline cervical incision was made. The ECA was separated and ligated. A rounded-tip 4-0 siliconized filament was inserted into the internal carotid artery and advanced to the origin of the right middle cerebral artery (MCA), approximately 18–22 mm from the insertion point, to produce a sudden drop in cerebral blood flow (CBF) to below 25% of baseline, as measured using a laser Doppler monitor (Periflux PF3, Stockholm, Sweden). Following MCAO, the rats were placed in temperature-controlled recovery cages for 2 hours to prevent post-surgery hypothermia. After 90 minutes, the occlusion suture was removed to allow reperfusion. Sham-operated rats underwent the same procedure as HT rats, without occlusion of the MCA. The survival rate in each group was monitored daily. Assessment of infarct volume and HT Infarct volume was calculated 5 days after MCAO, as described previously (Zhang et al., 2021). Brains were collected, frozen on dry ice, and serially sliced into five coronal sections (2-mm thick) using a mold for coronal brain slicing (RWD Life Science). The brain slices were stained with 1% 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC, Sigma) for 15 minutes. The cerebral infarct area was calculated using ImageJ software 6.0. The infarct volume was calculated using the following formula: the percentage of hemisphere lesion volume after edema correction = [total infarct volume – (ipsilateral hemisphere volume – contralateral hemisphere volume)]/contralateral hemisphere volume 100%. The stained brain sections were assessed for hemoglobin content via spectrophotometric assay (Bio-Rad xMark Microplate Spectrophotometer, Tokio, Japan) (Guo et al., 2016). After homogenization and centrifugation of brain tissue, the supernatant was collected. A 20-μL aliquot of supernatant was mixed with 80 μL of Drabkin reagent (Sigma), and the optical density (OD) at 540 nm was measured. A blinded investigator scored macroscopic HT (referred to as the HT index) in the brain slices (five stained brain sections) using a four-point rubric (Kelly-Cobbs et al., 2013): 0: no hemorrhage; 1: dispersed individual petechiae; 2: confluent petechiae; 3: small diffuse hemorrhage or hematoma ( 30% of the infarcted area); 4: large diffuse hemorrhage or hematoma ( 30% of the infarct volume). The total score for each rat was reported (score range, 0–20) and as the score increased, the degree of HT became more severe. Behavioral testing Neurological function was assessed by Garcia score (Garcia et al., 1995). The test was conducted after 1, 3, and 5 days of reperfusion. The Garcia score (Garcia et al., 1995) is a composite of six parts: spontaneous activity, symmetry of movements (four limbs), symmetry of forelimbs (outstretching while held by tail); vibrissa touch; body proprioception; and climbing capacity. Neurological function was graded on a scale of 0 to 18 points (normal score, 18; maximal deficit score, 3). As the score decreased, the injury became more severe. Sensorimotor deficits were assessed 2 and 4 days after MCAO by the contact and removal adhesive tape test (Luo et al., 2020). Briefly, the rats were placed in a clear plexiglass box and allowed to explore the new environment for 2 or 3 minutes. A black adhesive label 10 mm in diameter was placed on the inside surface of each forelimb. Then the rats were returned to the plexiglass box, , and the time point (Contact time) when the mouse's mouth first contacted the tape and the time point (Remove time) when the tape was torn off were recorded. Post-MCAO trials were conducted twice for 180 s each time to diminish stress effects related to handing. The results are expressed as the mean of the two trials of either the contact time or the removal time. The two neurobehavioral tests were performed by investigators blinded to the group assignments. Statistical analysis No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes; however, our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications (Xu et al., 2020; Kawabata et al., 2022). Data were analyzed using SPSS software 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and GraphPad Prism 9 (San Diego, CA, USA). A P value 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All of the data were tested for normality and variance homogeneity. Statistically significant differences among the three groups were determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc Tukey's multiple comparison test. Statistical comparisons between two groups were performed by Student's t -test. Nonparametric analyses were performed by Mann-Whitney U test (two groups) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test (three groups). The baseline characteristics of included patients are presented as numbers (%), and continuous variables with normal distributions are presented as the mean ± SD, while other variables that were not normally distributed are shown as the median (IQR). Patient characteristics were compared using the Pearson's chi-square test for trend for categorical data, one-way ANOVA for normally distributed continuous data followed by the LSD test (equal variances assumed) or Tamhance's T2 test (equal variances not assumed), and Kruskal-Wallis H test for non-normally distributed continuous data. Spearman's correlation coefficient was used to analyze the association between the gut microbiota and plasma biomarkers. Results Participant characteristics A total of 48 participants were included in this study ( Table 1 ). Fifteen patients with hemorrhagic transformation after stroke and 17 age- and sex-matched patients with AIS but without HT were included in the study. The patients in both the HT and the non-HT group had similar age and sex distributions compared with the control group. As expected, compared with non-HT patients, patients with HT presented with a more severe stroke (assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, NIHSS) ( P = 0.005). The systolic blood pressure (SBP) at admission was significantly higher in patients with HT compared with patients in the HC group ( P = 0.006). A recent study showed that a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio predicts HT after large atherosclerotic infarction in patients with acute ischemic stroke (Zhang et al., 2020). Consistent with this, our results showed that the neutrophil concentration and the N to L ratio were higher in the HT group compared to the HC group ( P = 0.027 and P = 0.005, respectively). The N to L ratio was higher in the HT group compared to the non-HT group ( P = 0.012), suggesting that inflammation was associated with HT. Three participants were excluded due to a low number of microbiome sequencing reads, resulting in a total of 43 participants included in the sequencing analyses described below. Gut microbiota profile of study participants In total, 3,659,508 reads with read counts averaging 83,316 reads per sample were denoised and merged and survived chimera filtering. We used two metrics to assess gut microbiota diversity: alpha- (i.e., a within-sample metric) and beta- (i.e., a between-sample metric) diversity. As shown in Figure 2 A and B , compared to the controls, alpha and beta diversity were decreased in both the non-HT and HT groups. However, we did not observe any difference in alpha and beta diversity between the non-HT and HT groups. The overall microbial composition of the gut microbiota in the HT and non-HT groups is shown at the family, genus, species, and phylum levels ( Figure 2 D , F , H , and Additional Figure 1B ). The three largest phyla in the healthy control, HT, and non-HT groups were Firmicutes , Proteobacteria , and Bacteroidetes , while Pseudomonadaceae , Lachnospiraceae , and Enterobacteriaceae were the most abundant families ( Figure 2 D and Additional Figure 1B ). A ternary plot of phylum, family, and genus distribution across the three groups showed that Proteobacteria , Enterobacteriaceae , and Escherichia-Shigella (these three species belong to the same branch of the phylogenetic tree) were relatively more abundant in the HT group than in the other two groups ( Figure 2 C and E , and Additional Figure 1A ). At the species level, E. coli was the predominate taxon in HT subjects ( Figure 2 G ). Species with significant differences ( P 0.05) among groups are marked with an asterisk. Compared to the HC group, increased abundance of the phylum Proteobacteria ( P = 0.015) and decreased abundances of the phyla Bacteroidota ( P = 0.021) and Actinobacteriota ( P = 0.024) were detected in the HT group ( Additional Figure 1B ). There were also some differences in phylum abundance between HT and non-HT subjects. Chloroflexi ( P = 0.003), Myxococcota ( P = 0.002), Acidobacteriota ( P = 0.048), and unidentified_ Bacteria ( P = 0.007) were increased, while the relative abundance of Campylobacterota ( P 0.001) was decreased, in HT subjects compared with non-HT subjects ( Additional Figure 1B ). At the family level, we found increased relative abundance of Enterobacteriaceae ( P = 0.064) and decreased abundance of Muribaculaceae ( P = 0.023) and Lachnospiraceae ( P = 0.002) in HT subjects compared with non-HT subjects ( Figure 2 D ). Significantly increased relative abundance at the genus and species level was seen for Escherichia-Shigella ( P = 0.03) and E. coli. ( P = 0.025), respectively, in the HT group compared with the non-HT group ( Figure 2 F and H ). Some specific taxa were even more prevalent in the non-HT group or in the HT group compared with the healthy control group, as defined by a linear discriminant analysis score higher than 3.5 in the healthy control, non-HT, or HT group ( Figure 3 A and B ). This cutoff value was chosen specifically to identify taxa that were likely to have biological significance instead of just a significant P value. We found that healthy subjects had higher levels of anti-inflammatory microbiome taxa than HT subjects, including Ruminococcaceae , Acidobacteriota , Faecalibacterium , and Clostridiales , while compared to healthy subjects, non-HT subjects had higher levels of Streptococcus , Fusicatenibacter , and Pectobacterium , and HT subjects had higher levels of Lactobacillus_salivarius and Klebsiella ( Figure 3 A and B ). To identify taxa that accounted for the major differences among these three groups, we performed similarity percentage analysis to determine the sample dissimilarity contribution ( Figure 3 C and D ). Enterobacteriaceae at the family level and Escherichia-Shigella at the genus level mostly accounted for the major differences between the HT and non-HT groups. Network analysis also identified co-occurrence of bacterial taxa in different states ( Additional Figure 2 ). As shown in Additional Figure 2A , the network in HC subjects was dominated by beneficial Firmicutes . However, a highly complex network of interactions was found in the non-HT and HT groups ( Additional Figure 2B and C ). The network in HT subjects was dominated by a chain of hub genera classified as Proteobacteria. Escherichia, which is a type of LPS-producing bacteria, were significantly increased and co-occurred with different bacteria in the HT network. A previous study (Levy and Borenstein, 2013) proposed that positive and negative correlations represent metabolic complementarity and competition, respectively, suggesting that LPS-producing bacteria have a competitive survival advantage in HT subjects. Microbial translocation and inflammatory response In addition to changes in the gut microbiota, stroke patients who develop HT exhibit barrier dysfunction. Stroke patients with HT demonstrated significantly increased plasma MMP9 levels compared with non-HT subjects ( P = 0.034; Figure 4 A ). Similarly, the plasma zonulin concentration was increased in the HT group ( P = 0.029; Figure 4 B ), suggesting brain and gut barrier dysfunction. As a consequence of gut leakiness, microbial LPS released into the tissues further activates the TLR4 pathway in immune cells, promoting systemic inflammation and neuroinflammation (Wasiak and Gawlik-Kotelnicka, 2023). We quantified plasma levels of LPS as a maker of microbial translocation. Higher plasma LPS levels were observed in HT subjects compared with non-HT subjects ( P 0.05; Figure 4 C ). Furthermore, plasma sCD14 and LBP levels were different in the HT group compared with the non-HT group ( Figure 4 D and E ), although these differences were not significant ( Figure 4 F ). Next, we analyzed the associations between biomarker measurements and the gut microbiota. As can be seen in Figure 5 A , plasma LPS ( r = 0.382, P = 0.012) and zonulin ( r = 0.323, P = 0.034) levels correlated positively with the relative abundance of Escherichia-Shigella. In addition, we found a strong significant correlation between alpha diversity and LPS levels, as well as LBP levels ( Figure 5 B ). Higher zonulin levels were negatively associated with Simple and Shannon index values ( Figure 5 B ). Thus, it is reasonable to conclude that the LPS-related microbiota is associated with HT after stroke. To determine whether predicted biological pathways with high sample prevalence rather than specific types of bacteria were associated with HT, we passed QIIME-outputted amplicon sequence variant tables through the PICRUSt server to predict activated pathways based on highly expressed genes ( Figure 5 C ). We identified 97 predicted microbiome gene pathways that were different in the HT group compared with the non-HT group, including 83 that were upregulated and 14 that were downregulated. Particularly relevant were the upregulation of genes involved in the oxidative phosphorylation and biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, which are relevant to cardiovascular disease and stroke. The PPAR signaling pathway, associated with both LPS and HT, was also upregulated in the HT group. Moreover, we observed a nonsignificant trend toward an increase in LPS-related functional pathways (LPS biosynthesis and LPS biosynthesis proteins) in HT participants compared to HC and non-HT subjects ( Figure 5 D and E ). Microbiota-based regulation of HT Consisted with our clinical findings from the current study, we previously reported that the relative abundances of Proteobacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, and Escherichia were also significantly increased in MCAO rats with hemorrhagic transformation (Huang et al., 2021). To determine the role of the gut microbiota and LPS-associated inflammation in HT, we used an HT model ( Figure 6 A ). Blood glucose levels were monitored throughout surgery in the HT and non-HT groups ( Figure 6 B ). The HT group exhibited a significantly larger infarct size ( P = 0.005; Figure 6 D ) and severer neurological dysfunction compared with the non-HT group ( Figure 6 F ). Consistent with this, the hemoglobin content was higher in HT group than in non-HT group ( P = 0.023; Figure 6 E ). Additionally, motor and sensory impairment were evaluated by the adhesive removal test at two different time points (days 2 and 4; Figure 6 G and H ). The HT group exhibited significantly increased contact time with the stickers ( Figure 6 G ) and a longer time until removal of the stickers ( Figure 6 H ). Regarding inflammatory factors, HT induced by hyperglycemia increased plasma LPS ( P = 0.04), LBP, and sCD14 ( P 0.01) levels in the rat model, similar to our clinical findings ( Figure 6 I–K ). Compared with the non-HT group, HT triggered an increase in LPS ( P = 0.039) and sCD14 ( P 0.01) concentrations but no statistically significant change in LBP concentration ( Figure 6 I–K ). Furthermore, the mortality rate on the 5 th day was higher in the HT group than in the non-HT group ( P = 0.026; Figure 6 C ). To confirm the role of the gut microbiota, we performed fecal transplants from HG and NG rats to another group of rats depleted of gut bacteria and then induced HT (F-HT, F-non-HT) ( Figure 7 A ). The glucose level at the time of MCAO was not significantly different between the F-HT group and the F-non-HT group ( Figure 7 B ). Compared with the F-non-HT group, microbiota transplant from HT rats induced an increase in infarct volume ( P = 0.034), HT index ( P 0.01), and hemoglobin level ( P = 0.023; Figure 7 D–F ). The rats in the F-HT group exhibited markedly worse performance in the adhesive removal test compared with the rats in the F-non-HT group ( Figure 7 G–I ). Microbiota transplant from HT rats triggered higher plasma levels of LPS ( P 0.01), LBP ( P = 0.022), and sCD14 ( P 0.01) in plasma ( Figure 7 J–L ). Unsurprisingly, the mortality rate was higher in the FMT-HG group, although this difference was not statistically significant ( P = 0.4; Figure 7 C ). Discussion Here, we combined gut microbiota sequencing and LPS, LBP, and sCD14 quantification with HT monitoring in a retrospective clinical cohort. We found that the gut microbiota in the HT and non-HT groups was different from that in healthy subjects in terms of both diversity and composition. There were some specific bacteria associated with the HT group, such as increased abundance of Escherichia-Shigella and E. coli . Moreover, we found that HT participants had higher plasma levels of LPS, LBP, and sCD14. We also performed fecal microbiota transplant in rats and verified the role of the gut microbiota in HT. Taken together, our findings show that LPS-induced inflammatory pathways activated by the gut microbiota in HT patients may increase the risk of developing HT and could help develop new therapeutic approaches for hemorrhagic transformation. This bidirectional communication, termed the gut-brain axis, provides novel avenues for both the prevention and treatment of stroke (Clottes et al., 2023). In accordance with prior studies, we observed changes in microbial alpha and beta diversity between the HC and non-HT or HT groups. Although we did not identify changes in diversity between the non-HT and HT groups, we did identify taxa with differential prevalence. Particularly relevant are the higher levels of Escherichia-Shigella and E. coli observed in HT subjects. Enterobacteriaceae are known as LPS-producers and have been previously positively associated with stroke in other cohorts (Kurita et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021). Our sequencing results showed that the relative abundance of Escherichia was significantly higher in HT subjects than in non-HT subjects. In addition, FMT from HT donors aggravated infarct severity to a certain extent in rats that underwent MCAO. It has previously been reported that the microbiota plays a vital role in stroke (Guo et al., 2021) and its complications, including stroke depression (Jiang et al., 2021), cognitive impairment (Ling et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020), and infection (Oh and Parikh, 2022). Therefore, the data presented here add to our understanding of the microbiota-based response to stroke outcomes. Gut microbial metabolites are key for gut microbiota-host communication (Liu et al., 2022; Kang et al., 2023). We found that the LPS biosynthesis pathway was upregulated in HT subjects, although this difference was not statistically significant. Indeed, we found higher levels of LPS and LBP in HT subjects. LBP is produced by hepatic and gastrointestinal epithelial cells in response to LPS stimulation (Molinaro et al., 2020). LBP and sCD14 are acute phase proteins that are considered markers of LPS bioactivity (Molinaro et al., 2020). In response to an inflammatory stimulus, LBP binds to LPS and delivers it to CD14, which is a pattern-recognition receptor associated with E. coli that participates in LPS signaling (Laugerette et al., 2014). In our study, compared with the non-HT and healthy controls, HT subjects had higher LPS and LBP levels, demonstrating that LPS-induced inflammation is associated with HT. Furthermore, we verified the role of the gut microbiota and LPS in HT through microbial transplantation. The “conventionalized” rats (whose gut flora was rescued) showed increased plasma LPS and LBP levels. Our results link endotoxin-related inflammation to the risk of HT and gut dysbiosis after stroke, although evidence for a causal link among these factors requires further exploration. Apart from LPS, the gut microbiota generates biologically active metabolites that regulate many aspects of host physiology (Cuciniello et al., 2023), highlighting the power of untargeted metabolomics and targeted metabolomics to identify gut-derived metabolites and new mechanisms of disease. Further efforts to integrate metabolomics with genomics and other “omics” data sets could yield new information about potential pathways regulating the development of HT after stroke. The integrity of the barriers that surround the brain and the gut mediates neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation after stroke (Zhu et al., 2020). The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is considered the gatekeeper of the CNS, and its main role is to maintain the fragile homeostasis of the brain (Halder et al., 2023). The cascade related to reperfusion injury and oxidative stress, leukocyte infiltration, and dysregulated extracellular proteolysis contributes to HT by undermining the integrity of the BBB (Bernardo-Castro et al., 2023). High MMP9 levels have been identified as an independent predictive factor for HT in stroke patients (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2023). In addition, it has become increasingly evident that stroke alters gut motility and increases gut permeability (Lee et al., 2020), which allows LPS to enter the bloodstream and activate vascular inflammation (Brown and Hazen, 2015). Recently, Carloni et al. (2021) reported that bacteria-derived LPS contributes to deregulation of the gut-brain vascular barrier and inflammatory bowl disease-related mental symptoms. Zonulin, a 47-kDa protein initially described by Wang et al. (2000), functions as an endogenous regulator of intestinal paracellular permeability by disassembling tight junctions (TJs). Skardelly et al. (2009) demonstrated that zonulin can increase BBB permeability. Elevated plasma zonulin levels have been reported in patients with neurological disease such as multiple sclerosis (Camara-Lemarroy et al., 2020) and Alzheimer's disease (Karim et al., 2022). However, a study based on a total of 217 subjects with neurological conditions found no evidence for a significant contribution of zonulin to increased BBB permeability (Stuart et al., 2022). Other indirect pathways such as gastrointestinal permeability linked with the gut-brain axis are more likely to be responsible for this phenomenon. Of note, we found that both zonulin and MMP9 levels were decreased in stroke patients with HT, suggesting possibly compromise of the intestinal and brain barriers. Future studies should assess intestinal barrier and BBB permeability using more precise methods. More research is required to determine how HT-induced changes in specific components of the gut microbiota and LPS affect the integrity of the BBB and the intestinal barrier. Our study had some limitations. This was a single-center study with a relatively small sample size. However, our results are consistent with previous studies that explored risk factors for HT. As our cohort did not include patients with diabetes, a major comorbidity of stroke (especially LAA subtypes), our results showing the relationship between the gut microbiota and HT are robust and valid. Albeit modest, our study took advantage of a patient cohort and an animal model of stroke, which allowed us to determine microbial associations with HT. In conclusion, our findings provided observational evidence of alterations in the composition of the gut microbiome in patients who develop HT after stroke. The plasma LPS concentration was increased. This suggests that targeting LPS and the specific bacteria identified here may represent a new avenue for preventing or treating HT in stroke patients. Rett syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder affecting 1 in 10,000 live female births. Changes in microbiota composition, as observed in other neurological disorders such as autism spectrum disorders, may account for several symptoms typically associated with RTT. We studied the relationship between disease phenotypes and microbiome by analyzing diet, gut microbiota, and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. We enrolled eight RTT patients and 10 age- and sex-matched healthy women, all without dietary restrictions. The microbiota was characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and SCFAs concentration was determined by gas chromatographic analysis. The RTT microbiota showed a lower α diversity, an enrichment in Bacteroidaceae , Clostridium spp., and Sutterella spp., and a slight depletion in Ruminococcaceae . Fecal SCFA concentrations were similar, but RTT samples showed slightly higher concentrations of butyrate and propionate, and significant higher levels in branched-chain fatty acids. Daily caloric intake was similar in the two groups, but macronutrient analysis showed a higher protein content in RTT diets. Microbial function prediction suggested in RTT subjects an increased number of microbial genes encoding for propionate and butyrate, and amino acid metabolism. A full understanding of these critical features could offer new, specific strategies for managing RTT-associated symptoms, such as dietary intervention or pre/probiotic supplementation.
